32.1 i ntroduction
In Chapter 31, we extended regression from the simple linear case, in which the dependent
variable is related to a single predictor, to multiple linear regression, which involves two or
more predictors. Similarly, we perform analysis of variance when a dependent variable is
affected by two or more factors. In this chapter, we investigate two-way analysis of variance
and discuss how factors can be employed as an experimental control.
The following example involves an analysis of variance in which the dependent variable is
affected by two factors.

If there is significant interaction between the factors, we cannot draw reliable conclusions
about their individual effects on the dependent variable. Therefore, we look first at the F sta-
tistic associated with the interaction sum of squares. At the 5% significance level, the critical
F value corresponding to 6 degrees of freedom in the numerator and 24 in the denominator
is 2.51. The F statistic for interaction is 0.33, less than the critical value, so at a = 5% we can-
not conclude that the two factors interact to affect sales. We examine the other F statistics
to test the row and column effects.

The two-way ANOVA: Without Replication function is available under Data Analysis as a selection
under the Tools menu. This function does not test for interaction and therefore, the author
recommends executing two-way ANOVA problems utilizing a standard statistical package, such as
SPSS.
Analyses of variance involving two or more factors can be performed in SPSS with the
procedure ANOVA (which also performs one-way tests). This example program using the
American Cities database in Appendix B groups the values of X7 in order to use it as a
factor, then performs a two-way analysis of variance to determine if X3 (unemployment)
is affected by X1 and X7.
Table 32.5 EXCEL two-way ANOVA printout.
None of the computed F statistics is significant, so we do not reject any of the null hypotheses in the
three tests that this analysis performs. We cannot conclude that the mean values of X3 change across
X1 or X7, or that X3 is affected by an interaction of X1 and X7. Note that the main effects are the row
and column effects.

32.3 r andomized-b lock d esigns
In the ANOVA designs considered thus far, the experimental units have been randomly assigned
to each factor level, and we have been interested in the effects on the dependent variable of
all the factors in the experiment. Such experimental designs are called completely randomized.
If an experiment includes two factors of which only one is to be investigated, the effect of the
“uninteresting” factor can be controlled through the use of a randomized-block design.
In the example in Table 32.12, a researcher investigates the mean lifetimes of spark plugs of
several brands (with the mean lifetimes the factor of interest), while controlling for the types
of cars used in the tests.
